h1: Rye malt and the sticky mash
title: Rye Malt and the Sticky Mash | Craft Beer School
desc: Why rye malt makes a sticky mash, the rests, rice hulls and enzymes that keep run-off moving and a 1,000 litre worked grist with 30% rye.
teaser: Rye gives beer a spicy, dry bite. It also gives your lauter tun a very bad afternoon if you treat it like barley.
standfirst: Rye malt is one of the most rewarding grains to brew with and one of the most awkward to lauter. The stickiness has clear causes and clear fixes. Here is how to brew with rye without a stuck mash.
sections: Why rye mashes turn to glue

Rye has no husk. Like wheat, it adds starch and flavour but nothing to build a filter bed. That alone makes lautering harder as the share of rye rises.

The bigger problem is gums. Rye is rich in pentosans, mainly arabinoxylans, plus beta-glucans. These long-chain carbohydrates dissolve into the mash and make the wort viscous. Thick wort runs slowly through the bed, pulls fine particles down onto the false bottom and compacts the grain. The result is the classic stuck rye mash: a slow trickle, a falling bed and a brewer reaching for the rake.
How much rye you can get away with

Weyermann's Pale Rye malt is listed at 4 to 10 EBC, with extract of at least 81% and a recommended addition of up to 60%, with an adapted, intensive mash. In practice:

  • Up to about 15% rye: most brewhouses manage with a normal single infusion and a slower run-off.
  • 15 to 30% rye: plan a gum rest and rice hulls.
  • Above 30% rye: use every tool (enzymes included) and expect longer lautering.

Our guide to Weyermann Pale Rye malt covers the full spec sheet.

A rest at about 40 to 45 °C lets the malt's own beta-glucanase enzymes break down beta-glucans before the mash goes up to saccharification temperature. Pentosans are harder to break down, but a rest in the same zone also gives some of the malt's cell wall enzymes time to work.

Hold for 15 to 20 minutes, then step up to your normal saccharification rest. At the end, mash out at 76 to 78 °C. Hot wort is thinner than cool wort, so a proper mash-out helps run-off more than most brewers expect. Our guide to enzymes in the mash explains how each enzyme responds to temperature.

Rice hulls replace the husk that rye lacks. They add no flavour or extract, only structure. A common dose is around 3 to 5% of grist weight at 30% rye or more. India has an advantage here: rice husk is widely available from rice mills. Buy clean, food-grade hulls if you can. Rinse them before use to remove dust and any off-flavours.

Exogenous enzymes, such as commercial beta-glucanase and xylanase blends, break down the gums more completely than the malt can on its own. They are widely used for high-rye or high-adjunct brewing. Follow the supplier's dose and temperature range. Our guide to stuck mash fixes covers what to do if the bed sticks anyway.
A worked 30% rye grist for 1,000 litres

Here is a rye ale at about 14 °P for a 1,000 litre batch, assuming roughly 68% of malt weight ends up as extract in the wort.

  • Pilsner malt: 110 kg (50%)
  • Pale rye malt: 66 kg (30%)
  • Munich malt Type 1: 33 kg (15%)
  • CARARYE: 11 kg (5%)
  • Total: 220 kg (100%)

Add about 7 to 11 kg of rice hulls. Mash in at 45 °C for 20 minutes, raise to 66 °C for 60 minutes, then mash out at 78 °C. Run off slowly, especially at the start. Watch the pressure difference across the bed. The beer should finish dry and spicy with a fuller body than its gravity suggests.

Rye kernels are smaller and harder than barley. A mill set for barley may leave many rye kernels uncracked. Some brewers mill rye separately with a tighter gap. Check the milled grist: you want the rye kernels broken, not passing through whole.

On run-off, start slowly and recirculate until the wort runs clear. Keep the bed covered with liquid. Rake gently if your lauter tun has rakes, but avoid cutting too deep. A rye mash that runs off in 90 minutes instead of 60 is normal. One that stops completely is a sign to look at the rest, the hulls or the mill.
Know your mash before you scale up

The 6% moisture limit on pale rye also matters in India. Rye picks up humidity in the monsoon months and mills less cleanly when damp. Store it sealed and use opened bags first.

Brewing with rye well means understanding mash enzymes, viscosity and lautering together. That combination is where a structured course earns its place.

Your first step: brew your house pale ale with 15% rye malt and record the run-off time against your normal batch. Then decide how far to push the rye.
faqs: Why does rye make a sticky mash?
Rye is rich in pentosans and beta-glucans that make wort viscous. It also has no husk to build a filter bed.
How much rye can I use without problems?
Up to about 15% usually runs off with a normal mash. Above that, plan a gum rest and rice hulls.
What temperature is a gum rest?
About 40 to 45 °C for 15 to 20 minutes, before stepping up to saccharification.
How many rice hulls should I add?
Around 3 to 5% of grist weight at 30% rye or more. Rinse them before use.
